claims.claim: Engineering design is the process of devising a system, component, or process to meet desired needs and specifications within constraints, applying basic science, mathematics, and engineering science to convert resources into solutions.

Science, engineering, and technology are distinct: science refers to the natural sciences that investigate the world as it is; engineering is a systematic practice of design to achieve solutions to human problems; technology is the result of that practice, not only computers or electronic devices.
Engineering design is not merely applied science; engineering practice shares much with scientific practice but has a different purpose and a different product.

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics groups architecture and engineering occupations together and reports a May 2024 median annual wage of $97,310 for the group, against $49,500 for all occupations; overall employment in the group is projected to grow faster than the average for all occupations from 2024 to 2034, with about 186,500 openings projected each year on average.

BLS reported 368,900 civil engineering jobs in 2024, a projected 5 percent growth and an employment change of 18,500 over 2024-34, and a May 2024 median annual wage of $99,590; mechanical engineers numbered 293,100 in 2024 with 9 percent projected growth and a May 2024 median of $102,320.

Engineering technologists and technicians are a separate occupational group from engineers: BLS reports an associate's degree as the typical entry-level education for civil engineering technologists and technicians, 64,900 jobs in 2024, and a May 2024 median annual wage of $64,200, against a bachelor's degree and $99,590 for civil engineers.

BLS lists a bachelor's degree as the typical entry-level education for engineering occupations such as aerospace, biomedical, chemical, civil, computer hardware, electrical and electronics, environmental, industrial, materials, and mechanical engineering, and an associate's degree for the corresponding technologist and technician occupations.

The typical U.S. path to a Professional Engineer license runs through a bachelor's degree from an EAC/ABET-accredited program, the Fundamentals of Engineering exam, several years of acceptable progressive verifiable experience (commonly four), and the Principles and Practice of Engineering exam; licensing boards, not NCEES, issue licenses and set eligibility, and requirements vary by state or territory.

The FE exam is designed for students near the end of, or graduates of, an EAC/ABET-accredited undergraduate engineering program; it is a computer-based exam of 110 questions administered year-round at approved test centers, offered in several discipline-specific versions.

Licensure exists to protect the public: NCEES states its mission as advancing licensure for engineers and surveyors in order to safeguard the health, safety, and welfare of the public, and BLS notes that civil engineers typically must be licensed if they provide services directly to the public, with a PE able to approve design plans and sign off on projects.

Licensure is not required for every engineering job. Exemptions in state licensing laws place some individuals and organizations performing engineering services outside the licensing system; NSPE's position is that everyone in responsible charge of engineering practice that potentially affects public health, safety, and welfare should be required to be licensed, and it recommends eliminating those exemptions.

State licenses are issued individually, and most states recognize licensure from other states as long as the issuing state's requirements meet or exceed their own; some states require continuing education to maintain a license.

ABET is a nonprofit, non-governmental agency that accredits programs — not institutions — in applied and natural science, computing, engineering, and engineering technology through four commissions; its accreditation is voluntary, and as listed in August 2026 it covered 4,863 programs at 950 colleges and universities in 42 countries.

ABET distinguishes engineering programs, which focus more on theory and conceptual design and require higher-level mathematics, from engineering technology programs, which focus more on application and implementation; the Engineering Accreditation Commission accredits bachelor's and master's engineering programs while the Engineering Technology Accreditation Commission accredits associate and bachelor's engineering technology programs.

ABET's engineering student outcomes require graduates to be able to solve complex engineering problems using engineering, science, and mathematics; to apply engineering design with consideration of public health, safety, and welfare and of global, cultural, social, environmental, and economic factors; to communicate effectively with a range of audiences; to recognize ethical and professional responsibilities; to function effectively on a team; to develop and conduct experimentation and use engineering judgment; and to acquire and apply new knowledge.

Communication, teamwork, and balancing competing objectives are explicit parts of engineering work rather than incidental to it: BLS lists communication, decision-making and interpersonal skills as important qualities for civil engineers, including explaining projects to nontechnical audiences and balancing feasibility against cost and safety.

Civil engineers' listed duties include analyzing plans, survey reports, maps and other design data and analyzing test results on soil and building materials — analysis work distinct from producing a new design.

Arithmetic check on the BLS figures: 368,900 + 18,500 = 387,400 projected civil engineering jobs in 2034 (18,500/368,900 = 5.01%); 293,100 + 26,500 = 319,600 mechanical engineering jobs (26,500/293,100 = 9.04%); the group median of $97,310 is 1.97 times the all-occupations median of $49,500, a gap of $47,810; the civil engineer median of $99,590 is 1.55 times the $64,200 civil engineering technologist and technician median, a gap of $35,390.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many licensing boards NCEES comprises
positions: The NCEES licensure page refers to 69 member licensing boards representing the 50 states, D.C., Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
The NCEES about page describes member boards covering the same 55 jurisdictions but counted as 56 boards.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The two counts almost certainly reflect different countings of separate engineering and surveying boards within the same jurisdictions. Because the discrepancy could not be resolved from the sources read, the lesson states only that every U.S. state and territory has its own board and does not publish a board count.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How widespread the industrial exemption is
positions: Secondary summaries circulate specific counts of states with and without industrial exemptions.
The NSPE position statement that was actually read describes exemptions in current state licensing laws and recommends eliminating them, without a count this research could verify.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: No count is published in the lesson. The exemption is described qualitatively, attributed to NSPE's position statement, and readers are pointed to their own state board rather than given a number that could not be checked.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether engineering technology graduates can sit for the FE and PE
positions: NCEES describes the FE as designed for students and graduates of EAC/ABET-accredited programs.
Secondary sources claim a specific split of states that do and do not permit ETAC graduates to pursue the PE.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson says only that eligibility is set by each state board and varies, which NCEES states directly. The specific state counts were not verifiable from authoritative sources and are not published.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive claims at all: its prose was topic-agnostic boilerplate about defining a concept, using context, and applying it to an example, with the topic title substituted in.
The draft's vocabulary list defined 'What Engineers Do' circularly as 'a foundational Engineering Fundamentals concept covered in this lesson'.
The draft's worked example described a student reading a scenario rather than any engineering work.
The draft's question bank tested generic study strategy rather than any engineering content.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced every section with researched content about engineering as a discipline, not with generic concept-learning advice.
Added the science/engineering/technology distinction, which the draft omitted entirely.
Added the disciplines, the engineer/technologist/technician distinction, licensure, ABET accreditation, and the analysis/design split.
Added dated, executed-and-checked BLS employment and wage figures where the draft had none.
Added the explicit statement that this is educational material and not engineering design guidance, per the subject's safety caution.
Added an explicit no-career-advice and no-licensure-eligibility-advice statement and pointed readers to their own state licensing board.
Rewrote all five questions to test engineering substance, with keys and distractors checked against the evidence.
rightsIssues: BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook content is a U.S. government work and is in the public domain, with credit requested. BLS blocks automated retrieval, so the pages were read through Internet Archive captures of the same public pages (2026-08-09 for the group, civil engineers and mechanical engineers pages; 2026-07-05 for the civil engineering technologists and technicians page). All four carry a BLS last-modified date of 2025-08-28. Facts were synthesized; no BLS wording was reproduced.
NCEES, ABET, and NSPE pages state no reuse license. They are classified REFERENCE_ONLY: their facts are used, their wording is not reproduced.

The NSPE Code of Ethics for Engineers itself could not be retrieved (the code page returned 404 and the PDF returned 403), so no canon text is quoted or paraphrased in this lesson; the code is named only as something the ethics topic covers.
NGSS Appendix I is published by Achieve/NextGenScience and states no explicit reuse license on the PDF; it is classified REFERENCE_ONLY and its definitions were restated in original wording.
No engineering standard (ASME, ASTM, IEEE, ISO, ACI, AISC) text, table, or design value appears in this lesson.
